name: Goa
tagline: India's smallest state: palm-lined beaches, whitewashed Portuguese churches, spice plantations, seafood shacks and a laid-back rhythm that is unlike anywhere else in the country.
highlight: Fresh fish and a cold drink at a beach shack, watching the sun drop into the Arabian Sea.
shortDescription: A former Portuguese colony with 100 km of beaches, the UNESCO-listed churches of Old Goa, the Latin Quarter of Panjim, forts, markets and a food culture found nowhere else in India.
metaDescription: A Goa travel guide: North and South Goa beaches, Old Goa's churches, Fontainhas, Fort Aguada, spice plantations, Goan food, when to go and a four-day plan.
nearestAirport: Dabolim (GOI) or Manohar International at Mopa (GOX)
knownFor: Beaches, Portuguese heritage, seafood, nightlife, relaxed atmosphere
goodFor: Beaches, relaxation, food, nightlife, colonial heritage

image.alt: The curved sandy bay of Palolem beach in South Goa with palms and boats

intro: Goa was a Portuguese colony for about 450 years, from 1510 until India annexed it in 1961, which is much longer than the British ruled most of the subcontinent. The legacy is everywhere: in the Catholic churches, the Portuguese-style villas with balconies and tiled roofs, the food, the surnames and the relaxed attitude to alcohol and holidays. About a quarter of the population is Christian.

The coast is 100 km of sand, divided in practice into two. North Goa, around Baga, Calangute, Anjuna, Vagator and Arambol, is livelier, with markets, beach clubs and nightlife. South Goa, around Palolem, Agonda and Colva, is quieter, greener and more relaxed. Inland, rice fields, spice plantations, waterfalls and forest cover the Western Ghats.

Goa is best used as a place to rest, after the intensity of the north or as a beach stop on a longer trip. Its heritage is also worth seeing: the churches of Old Goa are a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the old quarter of Panjim, Fontainhas, is a maze of colourful Portuguese houses.

whyVisit.intro: Goa offers beaches, heritage and food on a compact coast, and is India's easiest place to unwind.

points.title: Beaches for all tastes
points.text: From party beaches with music to quiet coves and long open sands.

points.title: Portuguese heritage
points.text: Old Goa's churches, Fontainhas and colonial mansions.

points.title: Goan food
points.text: Fish curry rice, vindaloo, sorpotel and bebinca, with Portuguese, Konkani and Indian influences.

points.title: A relaxed pace
points.text: Beach shacks, yoga, cafés and markets, with less hassle than other parts of India.

points.title: Nature inland
points.text: Spice plantations, waterfalls and wildlife sanctuaries in the Western Ghats.

attractionsIntro: Split your time between the beach and the heritage sites, and choose your side of the coast.

attractions.name: The churches of Old Goa

image.file: File:Front Elevation of Basilica of Bom Jesus.jpg
image.alt: The laterite façade of the Basilica of Bom Jesus in Old Goa

attractions.text: The former Portuguese capital, now a UNESCO site, with the Basilica of Bom Jesus, which holds the remains of St. Francis Xavier, and the huge Sé Cathedral. Most of the city itself has vanished, but the churches remain.
attractions.tip: Go in the morning, and dress modestly.

attractions.name: Fontainhas, Panjim
attractions.text: The Latin Quarter of Goa's capital, with narrow lanes of pastel houses, small chapels and cafés, and a preserved Portuguese atmosphere.
attractions.tip: Walk in the late afternoon and stop for a coffee.

attractions.name: Fort Aguada

image.alt: The old Portuguese Fort Aguada and its lighthouse above the sea

attractions.text: A well-preserved 17th-century Portuguese fort on a headland north of Panjim, with a lighthouse and views along the coast.

attractions.name: Palolem and South Goa beaches
attractions.text: A crescent of white sand fringed by palms and fishing boats, with quiet neighbours such as Agonda and Patnem.
attractions.tip: Stay a few nights in South Goa.

attractions.name: Baga, Calangute and Anjuna
attractions.text: The lively northern beaches, with shacks, water sports, clubs and the famous Wednesday flea market at Anjuna.
attractions.tip: Go for the atmosphere, but be aware of crowds in the high season.

attractions.name: A spice plantation
attractions.text: Working farms inland where you can see pepper, cardamom, vanilla and cashew, and eat a traditional lunch.

thingsToDoIntro: Goa is a beach destination first, with plenty of options for the days in between.

thingsToDo.title: Eat at a beach shack
thingsToDo.text: Simple seafood restaurants on the sand, serving grilled fish, prawns and cold beer.

thingsToDo.title: Take a spice plantation tour
thingsToDo.text: A guided walk through a working farm, followed by a Goan lunch.

thingsToDo.title: Walk through Fontainhas
thingsToDo.text: Explore the old Portuguese quarter, with its colour and small chapels.

thingsToDo.title: Try water sports or a dolphin cruise
thingsToDo.text: Boat trips from Sinquerim and Palolem spot dolphins in the morning.

thingsToDo.title: Do a yoga class
thingsToDo.text: Yoga is popular in Goa, from drop-in classes to retreats.

thingsToDo.title: Visit a Saturday night market
thingsToDo.text: Night markets sell clothes, crafts and food, with live music.

foodIntro: Goan food mixes Portuguese and Konkani traditions, with coconut, vinegar, chilli and seafood.

foods.name: Goan fish curry rice
foods.text: The staple lunch: fish in a tangy, coconut-based curry with rice.

foods.name: Pork vindaloo and sorpotel
foods.text: Spicy, vinegary pork dishes with Portuguese origins.

foods.name: Prawn balchão and xacuti
foods.text: Prawns in a spicy pickle-like sauce, and chicken in a coconut and spice gravy.

foods.name: Bebinca
foods.text: A many-layered sweet of egg yolks, coconut milk and sugar.

foods.name: Poi and pao
foods.text: Soft local breads baked in wood ovens, eaten with curries or sausages.

foods.name: Feni
foods.text: A local spirit distilled from cashew apples or coconut sap.

accommodation.intro: Choose the coast that matches your mood, and book early for December and January.

areas.name: North Goa (Baga, Anjuna, Vagator)
areas.text: Guesthouses, hotels and boutique stays near the beach.

areas.name: South Goa (Palolem, Agonda)
areas.text: Beach huts, guesthouses and small resorts.

areas.name: Panjim and Old Goa
areas.text: Boutique hotels in restored Portuguese houses.

gettingThere.intro: Goa has two airports and good rail links.

options.text: Dabolim (GOI) in the south and Manohar International (GOX) at Mopa in the north, which opened in 2023, connect to Indian cities and some international routes.
options.detail: Choose the airport nearest your beach.

options.text: The Konkan Railway links Goa with Mumbai (about 10 to 12 hours) and Kerala.
About 9 to 12 hours from Mumbai or Pune, and about 6 to 8 hours from Hampi.

gettingAround.intro: Goa is small but spread out, and public transport is limited.

options.text: The most popular way to get around, at a low price.
options.detail: Wear a helmet, carry a licence and take care with traffic.

options.text: Prepaid taxis and app-based services operate.
Local buses cover the main routes.

bestTime.headline: November–February
bestTime.summary: Goa has a tropical climate, with a strong monsoon from June to September.

seasons.text: Dry, sunny and warm. Peak season, with Christmas and New Year very busy.
Hot and humid, and many places start closing.
Heavy rain, rough seas, and most beach shacks closed. The landscape is lush and prices are low.
Green, warm and quiet, as the season begins.

bestTime.avoid: The monsoon, when the sea is dangerous for swimming, and Christmas and New Year unless you love crowds.

itinerary.title: Four days in Goa
itinerary.intro: Heritage and the north, then a slower stay in the south.

tipsIntro: Goa is relaxed, and a few tips help.
tips: Choose your beach according to your mood: North for activity and South for quiet.
Wear a helmet if you rent a scooter, and carry a valid licence.
Swim only where lifeguards are present, and avoid the sea in the monsoon.
Book in advance for Christmas and New Year.
Watch out for touts and overcharging at beach shacks.

faq.a: North Goa for nightlife, markets and activity, and South Goa for quieter beaches and a relaxed atmosphere.

faq.q: How many days do you need in Goa?
faq.a: Four or five days for the coast and heritage sites.

faq.q: What is the best time to visit Goa?
faq.a: November to February. The monsoon closes many beach shacks.
It is a relaxed destination, but take care with scooters, sea currents and petty theft, and keep an eye on your drinks.

faq.q: Can I drink alcohol in Goa?
faq.a: Yes, it is widely available and cheaper than in most of India.
Mopa (GOX) is closer to North Goa, and Dabolim (GOI) is closer to Panjim and South Goa.
